notes.meaning: This is the heading for the list of priests in verses 1-19. The writer starts at the very beginning, with Aaron's four sons. Here "divisions" does not mean quarrels. It means sharing out the work so each group knew its turn. God is a God of order, not confusion, especially in worship.

Nadab and Abihu died while their father Aaron was still alive. God judged them for offering "strange fire," an offering he had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1-2). They left no sons, so the priesthood passed only through Eleazar and Ithamar. Eleazar later became high priest after Aaron, and his family held that office for a long time.

David did not do this alone. He worked together with two leading priests, Zadok from Eleazar's family and Ahimelech from Ithamar's family. Other books name Abiathar as Zadok's partner in David's day. Some teachers say this Ahimelech was Abiathar's son, named after his grandfather. Others say Abiathar also went by the name Ahimelech.

Eleazar's family had grown larger, so it had more family leaders. It got sixteen groups, and Ithamar's family got eight. Matthew Henry thinks Ithamar's line shrank after God's judgment on the family of Eli, who came from that line.

Both families had produced great leaders, even high priests, so neither could claim first place. Casting lots let God decide and kept anyone from being jealous or feeling cheated. The lot only settled the order of service. Every group still did the same work. As Proverbs says, the lot puts an end to quarrels.

A Levite scribe named Shemaiah wrote down each name as it was drawn. This was done in public, in front of the king and the leaders, so no one could suspect cheating. The lots seem to have been kept in two separate groups, one for each family, and drawn in turn. Bible teachers are not sure exactly how the drawing went once Ithamar's eight names ran out.

Here begins the list of the 24 priestly groups, called "courses," in the order the lots came out. Jehoiarib's group came first. Centuries later, the Maccabee family, who led a famous Jewish revolt, came from this group. Using the lot took away any reason for envy between the groups.

The list goes on with groups three to six. Little is known about most of these families beyond their names. The name Seorim does not appear anywhere else in the Bible. Mijamin may be another form of the name Benjamin.

Abijah's group came eighth. This is the "division of Abijah" in Luke 1:5. Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, belonged to it. So the groups David set up lasted, with breaks, all the way to New Testament times.

Groups nine to twelve are named here. Families from Jeshua's line were among those who came home after the exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:36). Eliashib means "God restores," and Jakim means "He will raise."
Groups thirteen to sixteen are named. Jeshebeab is not mentioned anywhere else. Immer's group, though, shows up often in later books of the Bible.
Groups seventeen to twenty are named. Happizzez is another name found only here. For many of these groups we know little more than the name.

The last four groups finish the list of 24. Jachin's group is mentioned often elsewhere. After the exile, only a few groups came back at first. Over time the system was rebuilt and the old names were carried on.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teachers link the 24 priestly groups with the 24 elders around God's throne in Revelation 4. They see both as standing for all of God's people.

notes.meaning: This was the order in which the groups took turns at God's house. Each group served for one week, from Sabbath to Sabbath. They followed the rules God had given through Aaron. "Aaron their father" means whoever was high priest at the time, since he stood in Aaron's place. Matthew Henry sees in this a picture of Christ, the great High Priest over all believers.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have argued that the 24 groups were really formed after the exile, and that the writer of Chronicles credited them to David. Older commentators reject this. They point to Ezekiel 8:16 and Nehemiah 12 as signs the groups existed earlier.

notes.meaning: Now the list turns to the other Levites. These were not priests, but they helped the priests in worship. They come from Kohath's son Amram. Shubael's family traced back to Moses' son Gershom, and Jehdeiah led that family in David's day.

Rehabiah's line was the second family from Moses' sons, and Isshiah led it. The Izharites were another Kohathite clan, led by Shelomoth and then Jahath. Many of these names already appeared in chapter 23. Here they show up again as heads of service groups.
Four leaders from Hebron's family are named in order. The Hebrew text here is a little damaged. English Bibles fill it in from the matching list in 1 Chronicles 23:19.
The last Kohathite clan comes from Uzziel. Micah and his son Shamir led one branch. Micah's brother Isshiah and his son Zechariah led another.

Next come the Levites from Merari's family, through Mahli and Mushi. Jaaziah is a name not found in earlier lists. "Beno" may not be a name at all, since in Hebrew it means "his son." Clarke notes that nothing is said here about Gershon's family.
Mahli's son Eleazar had no sons, so his line could not lead a group. Instead, Jerahmeel, the son of Mahli's other son Kish, is named as the leader.

Mushi's three sons close the list of Levite families. Many teachers think there were 24 Levite groups to match the 24 priestly groups, though they count the names in different ways. Gershon's family may be missing because it served elsewhere, such as guarding the temple treasures.

The Levites cast lots just as the priests had, in front of the king and the leaders. Each Levite group was paired with a priestly group to help it. Older and younger families drew on equal terms, so the lot, not age, set their place. Matthew Henry notes the priests are called the Levites' "brothers," not their lords. In Christ, younger and older are equally welcome.
